bibliographic.title: Why ML Models Fail to Reach Production
bibliographic.citation_apa: Oliveira, O. L. P. (2026). Why ML models fail to reach production. DOI: 10.66104/wbexse86

methodology.study_design: narrative review with documented database search strategy and grey literature from industry organizations
methodology.sample_description: Peer-reviewed literature and technical documentation from recognized industry organizations, identified via predefined query strings across three academic databases (2018-2025)
methodology.sector: cross-sector with illustrated cases in technology-adjacent organizations, large enterprises, and regulated financial sector
methodology.technology_context: MLOps, ML model lifecycle, deployment monitoring, tooling ecosystem; LLMOps subsection covering LLM pipelines, RAG, guardrails, and prompt management

eligibility.decision_rationale: The article is primarily a narrative bibliographic review on barriers to ML productionization and MLOps practices. It offers partial relevance through data governance failures, monitoring, deployment discipline, regulated financial sector cases, and a future-oriented LLMOps subsection mentioning RAG, guardrails, and human evaluation. However, it does not centrally address conversational governance, chatbots, agents, accountability/handoff/contestation in conversational systems, or regulated LLM conversational deployments. LLM content is confined mainly to section 10.1 and is operational rather than governance-of-conversation focused.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: Deterministic triage graded this as central_candidate (93.33) largely via broad keyword hits; manual adjudication is needed because conversational-AI relevance is weak (1/3) and LLM/guardrails/RAG content appears peripheral to the review's conversational governance scope.

appraisal.notes: Strengths include a clearly stated objective, explicit search strings, date bounds, and candid methodological caution about widely cited deployment-failure statistics. Limits include narrative rather than systematic review design, unclear final corpus size, no reported screening or quality appraisal of included sources, and no ethics/reflexivity discussion in the provided text.

cerqual.explanation: Findings are internally coherent for MLOps deployment barriers and operational practices, but the review method is narrative with incomplete reporting of inclusion counts and appraisal. Relevance to conversational LLM governance in regulated settings is partial and mostly indirect.

coding.theme: Operationalization and governance of ML/LLM systems in production
coding.subtheme: From classical MLOps to LLMOps for language models
rq_alignment: indirect support for operational governance, monitoring, and guardrails in LLM systems
limited alignment with conversational governance, human oversight/handoff, auditability, and regulated conversational AI

synthesis.main_claim: The primary determinant of ML success in production is not algorithmic sophistication, but organizational and engineering discipline around deployment, monitoring, and continuous improvement; MLOps addresses recurring barriers such as misalignment, data governance failures, weak testing, inadequate infrastructure, neglected monitoring, and organizational resistance.
synthesis.contribution: Maps seven deployment barriers, describes the ML production lifecycle and tooling ecosystem, and outlines incremental MLOps adoption strategies, with a forward-looking LLMOps discussion on prompt/RAG/guardrail operations for LLMs.
synthesis.limitations: Widely cited production-failure rates are survey-based and not validated longitudinally; the review is narrative rather than systematically reported; LLM/conversational governance content is brief and future-oriented.
synthesis.use_in_review: Use as supporting evidence for operational/technical governance of LLM deployment (monitoring, guardrails, RAG operations, human evaluation) and as contextual background on why governance and engineering discipline matter in regulated production settings; not suitable as central evidence on conversational governance.
